extracted.intended_audience: mathematicians and mathematically curious general readers (researchers, educators, and readers interested in the impact of AI on mathematical practice)
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and desiderata for what makes a mathematical proof "good" (beauty, insight, rigor, communication), with attention to how AI-produced proofs change what is valued. Useful for mathematicians, teachers, and readers judging or producing proofs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Elegance + Creativity + Beauty + Rigor
rubrics_metrics.description: "The best proofs are works of art. They're not just rigorous; they're elegant, creative and beautiful." Quality combines logical soundness with aesthetic and inventive elements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A top-quality proof must be logically sound (rigorous) while also exhibiting elegance and creativity — e.g., a simple, surprising argument or a clever idea that illuminates. Anti-patterns: mechanically correct but prosaic or opaque proofs that lack insight or aesthetic unity. Scoring note: reward concision, novelty of approach, and perceived aesthetic appeal alongside correctness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sturdy Foundation
rubrics_metrics.description: A proof requires "a rigorous, logical argument" built from "a sturdy foundation of assumptions, or axioms," with statements "placed... one at a time" in valid chains.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure every step follows validly from accepted premises; make assumptions explicit and avoid hidden leaps. Guidance emphasizes stepwise construction: statements should be placed one at a time so the chain of reasoning is transparent. Anti-patterns: glossing over foundational hypotheses or relying on unstated lemmas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Architectural Structure
rubrics_metrics.description: The overarching structure — "walls and stairs and columns" — gives proofs their shape and meaning; local validity is not enough; global form matters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess the proof's global organization: how lemmas, claims, and subarguments fit together to form a coherent whole. A well-structured proof guides the reader from assumptions to conclusion with clear scaffolding. Anti-patterns: isolated correct computations or local arguments that fail to assemble into an understandable global narrative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hands-Dirty Understanding
rubrics_metrics.description: Traditionally valued is knowing "every last detail" — getting "your hands dirty" with practical work rather than relying solely on abstractions — as essential to true comprehension.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Valuate proofs by whether the author (or reader) has engaged concretely with the material: worked examples, checked computations, and internalized mechanisms. Warning: over-reliance on abstraction or delegation (e.g., accepting machine output without verifying details) risks shallow understanding. Encourage doing the detailed work that reveals how and why a result holds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conceptual Insight Over Computation
rubrics_metrics.description: "Eureka moments" and the ability to make "an analogy or develop a new definition" are distinctly creative and valued above pure computation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize proofs that introduce new concepts, illuminating analogies, or conceptual simplifications over those that are merely heavy computation or routine verification. Scoring favors novelty of perspective, explanatory power, and the capacity to generalize. Anti-patterns: long, brute-force calculations that prove a fact but offer no new understanding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Communicative Clarity
rubrics_metrics.description: Emphasis on "providing explanations and conveying the most important ideas" rather than exhaustive detail — elegance includes effective communication of essential concepts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A good proof communicates: it highlights the key ideas, orients the reader, and balances detail with exposition. In the AI era, clarity and exposition may be more valuable than mechanically complete low-level derivations. Anti-patterns: proofs that bury the main idea in technical clutter or that are formally complete but unreadable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Did this proof teach me anything I didn't already know?
rubrics_metrics.description: Proposed new criterion: "Did this proof teach me anything I didn't already know?" — a measure of a proof's capacity to impart new understanding or surprise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use pedagogical/insight value as an evaluative axis: a proof that reveals new connections, simplifies understanding, or changes perspective scores highly. This criterion helps distinguish mechanically certified proofs (including AI-generated ones) from proofs that advance human understanding. Scoring note: subjective but important for assessing lasting value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Human judgment of beauty and insight (against AI limitations)
rubrics_metrics.description: AI can produce certified proofs but typically cannot identify which proofs are beautiful or insightful; mathematicians worry about losing the hands-dirty step.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that evaluation of aesthetic and conceptual value remains a human-centered task. When assessing proofs (especially AI-assisted ones), check for evidence of human understanding, explanatory choices, and insight rather than relying solely on formal certification. Anti-patterns: treating machine-verified derivations as equivalent to human-explained, insight-rich proofs.
